power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks 'chunk' word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval.
Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli.
How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence's component words in memory?

In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause.

Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall.

Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results.
We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

From very early in the study of memory, it has been understood that grouping stimuli into unitized representations can serve to augment short term memory accuracy (Cowan, 2001; Madigan, 1980; G. A. Miller, 1956).

text.text: In psycholinguistics, a classic body of prior research has asked how chunking processes work within sentences, which are internally organized and contain numerous sequential redundancies driven by both grammar and statistical patterns.
One influential prior hypothesis is that encoding processes align chunks with clause boundaries in short-term serial memory for sentences.

Early work in sentence comprehension hypothesized that clause boundaries served as cues to specialized processing, such as perceptual segmentation (Fodor & Bever, 1965), changes in depth of processing (Marslen-Wilson & Tyler, 1976), or the clearing of working memory (Jarvella, 1971).

text.text: Similarly, in the study of language production, there have been proposals that grammatical encoding proceeds in clause-sized units of planning (Bock & Cutting, 1992; Ford & Holmes, 1978).

text.text: In this study, we critically examine the evidence for the hypothesis that clause boundaries determine chunking in short term serial memory for sentences, with particular attention paid to serial recall accuracy near clause boundaries and item-order correlations.

A better understanding of how general mnemonic processes interact with specialized cognitive representations for sentences is crucial for developing more adequate theories of language comprehension (Lewis & Vasishth, 2005) and production (Bock et al., 2007).

text.text: We first describe some of the key metrics for chunking in serial recall tasks.
Chunking refers to a general process of working memory whereby a list of input stimuli is recoded from a larger number of unitary elements into a smaller number of abstract groupings.
Chunks may be based on familiar structures from long term memory, or an ad hoc grouping may be imposed at encoding.
A famous example of chunking using long term memory structures is the imposition of 'phone number' groupings onto digit strings.

When presented with the following list of seven digits: 3-5-7-1-1-1-3, a subject familiar with phone numbers standardized by the North American Numbering Plan may choose to recode these seven disparate digits into a 3 + 4 pattern, such as 375-1113.
Similarly, a more mathematically inclined subject may store this string programmatically as the first four prime numbers after the number two.
Chunking based on ad hoc grouping can be observed by simply directing participants to group a list with a certain strategy (3-4, 2-3-2, etc.; Farrell, 2008; Farrell et al., 2011).

text.text: Chunking of lists increases overall serial accuracy compared to unchunked lists, and the shape of the serial recall curve changes, where one may observe sharp changes in accuracy between chunks, though somewhat stable accuracy within chunks.
Discontinuities in average accuracy between potentially grouped positions is not the only metric that memory scientists apply for evaluating chunking strategies in serial recall of lists.
Another common metric is within-chunk serial position effects.

Since the early days of modern psychology, it has been known that in memorizing lists, memory tends to be most accurate for items in first and final positions (Calkins, 1896 https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?afwvQf  Madigan & O'Hara, 1992 for a historical review of this work).

text.text: When a chunking strategy is applied to a list in a serial recall task, primacy and recency effects can be observed within each chunk, leading to the appearance of a 'scalloped' serial recall curve across the list as a whole in which the beginning and final elements of each chunk are recalled with greater accuracy than the medial elements.
Consider a list composed of grouped digits and grouped letters, for example 794FWP.

Should a participant chunk this list into digits and lettershttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ozQbbc a scalloped serial accuracy curve will be observed with primacy and recency effects for each chunk This means that accuracy for 7 and 4 would be higher than that for 9, since this digit is medial to the first chunk, and accuracy for F and P would be higher than for W. Note that serial position effects within chunks are expected to be overlaid on global primacy and recency effects for the full list (Anderson & Matessa, 1997; Farrell, 2012) , such that in this example accuracy will also be heightened at the absolute beginning and ending elements, 7 and P.

Despite the same string-wise load of seven words, crossing a group/chunk boundary at encoding led to a large modulation in accuracy.

text.text: If clauses serve as chunks in the recall of sentences, we might also expect multi-clause sentences to demonstrate within-clause primacy and recency effects in addition to global primacy and recency effects at the sentence level.

Research in sentence recall in the 1970s did observe these effects, which manifested as scalloped recall curves by clause, similar to those seen for chunks in unstructured lists. Jarvella (1971) presented comprehenders with spoken passages of prose with periodic pauses, and instructed them that during these pauses they would be asked to write down the exact wording of the story they had heard just before the pause.

text.text: It should be noted that many of these results were found under narrative and discourse processing contexts, where the sentences tested are conceptually coherent at the clause and sentence level.

Were there evidence of similar grouping effects in the recall of isolated sentences, without narrative and discursive context, this would serve to suggest that there are at least some core mnemonic mechanisms underlying recall performance in both settings.
We now discuss a recent line of experimentation that discovers exactly this pattern.
Using simple auditory multi-clausal sentences of English, Roverud et al. (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jAl5KC) aimed to isolate the representational factors underlying sentence recall.
text.formatted: Using simple auditory multi-clausal sentences of English, Roverud et al. (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jAl5KC">2020</ref>) aimed to isolate the representational factors underlying sentence recall.

text.text: As grouping could arise by syntax, prosody, or semantics, the authors attempted to isolate syntactic organization by testing auditory sentence recall in prosodically and semantically impoverished stimuli.

To this end, the experiments their experiments use repetitive and semantically constrained stimuli, such as "JOHN BOUGHT TWO BIG BAGS IF MARY SAW THREE RED PENS BUT …", presented with list-like intonation rather than naturalistic prosody.
To further distinguish sentence-specific effects, the authors compare recall of syntactically well-formed strings with shuffled ungrammatical strings.
An effect of grammaticality is found in practically all positions, but most notable are the large primacy and recency effects by clause, what they term the clause boundary effect.
In their second experiment, the authors find that a clause boundary effect could be detected even when participants were prompted to complete recall backwards.

This is interpreted as evidence that syntactic structure at encoding leads to clausal organization at retrieval, even under different retrieval demands. Roverud et al. (2023) and Roverud & Kidd (2025) build on the clause boundary effect to investigate the interaction of clausal organization with various acoustic variables, using similar grammatical but constrained sentences, and again replicate the clause-by-clause recency and primacy effects.

text.text: Up to now, from the evidence we've reviewed across decades of experimental work, there seems no reason to doubt the conclusion that the scalloped clausal recall curves observed in the literature are a measure of clausal organization in memory.
However, the multiple, integrated levels of representation in natural language often result in strongly correlated factors across items and positions.

If scalloped recall curves are intended to serve as good evidence for abstract clause boundary effects, then we would wish to have evidence that no other incidentally correlated linguistic features could plausibly drive this change in accuracy.
In the next section we will argue that at least some of the previous claims of clause boundary effects are confounded in exactly this way, by consistently placing nouns at clause boundaries.
Serial position effects serve as strong evidence for clause-delimited chunking only if other factors affecting recall accuracy can be successfully dissociated from clause boundaries.

However in practice this can be challenging, as syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic constraints on grammatical utterances can easily lead to accidental correlations between serial position and other properties which do not arise for recall of unstructured word lists.

In this study we investigate whether the scalloped recall curves observed in the prior literature are a reflection of clausal memory units, or whether they may rather reflect a higher proportion of nouns at the beginning and ends of clauses.

Many theories of working memory rely on results from studies of arbitrarily ordered lists of words, which often motivate theories and models in which item and order information are assumed to then be representationally dissociable (Henson, 1998; Majerus, 2013; Nairne & Kelley, 2004; Oberauer et al., 2012).

These relative ordering constraints may be thought to transduce unordered hierarchical grammatical representations into linearized strings of words and phrases (Idsardi & Raimy, 2013; Kayne, 1994 Kayne, , 2022)).

text.text: Consider a simple case of English articles (a, the, those) and the nouns they form noun phrases with: nouns must linearly follow (rather than precede) the articles dependent on them (the dog, not dog the), though material may intervene (the tiny cute dog).
Here the serial position of an article in a grammatical utterance clearly limits the relative order of its head noun.
In the recall of sentences, retrieval of any single word thus serves to constrain the serial positions surrounding it, providing a kind of redundant cueing.
This even applies to some degree to linearly distant positions, as in the case of long distance dependencies.

That is, given the grammatical factors that systematically constrain word order in sentences, it is plausible that previously observed clause boundary effects are simply effects of syntactic and semantic constraints on particular positions which modulate recall accuracy, which happen to coincide with first and last clause positions, rather than more general effects of primacy and recency.
In this study we focus on the extent to which noun position correlates with clause edges in English.
English transitive declarative clauses have a canonical order of subject -verb -object, as in "Capybaras eat leafy plants and beavers eat tree bark".

Due to the head-final phrase structure of English noun phrases, the clause-ending object phrase will usually end with a noun, even when the noun is modified (plants in leafy plants; roots in leafy plants with roots).
This has the result that the last word of a transitive clause will often be a noun.

On the other end, while in English the subject phrase often begins with an article or quantifier (the women, most books), there are also many subject phrases that do not require articles, such as proper names ("Maryann went to the store") and bare plurals ("Pikas often squeak").
In these cases, the first word of the clause will also be a noun.
Thus in a conjoined multi-clause sentence such as "Kids like capybaras, but beavers are also growing in popularity", nouns begin and end each clause.

This potential correlation matters because evidence from previous research suggests that nouns are in fact memorized more accurately relative to other words (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?broken=8S1bMg. text.text: In their design, the unstructured word lists used as a baseline were created by scrambling the words of a well-formed sentence, such that they contained the same number of words per lexical class as their length-matched grammatical counterparts.
Therefore, Roverud et al. examined the effect of lexical category on accuracy in these scrambled sentence trials.
Their linear mixed model revealed no significant effect of lexical class on accuracy in these trials.
However, we argue that this result must be interpreted with caution.

The model fitted estimated a six-level category variable (names, verbs, numbers, adjectives, common nouns, conjunctions) with data from 10 participants, a sample size which may have been underpowered to detect significant differences in performance by lexical category.
Second, the task used was quite different from typical recall tasks.
The authors used closed lists of lexical items per category, such that each lexical category could be represented by one of only eight words.
For instance, the verb of any clause could be one of: bought, found, gave, held, lost, saw, sold, took.
After encoding, participants were cued for recall at each retrieval with the entire pool of words from a category, in the order they were encoded.

For example, if participants were recalling the grammatical sentence "Bob bought two big bags", they would first see the closed list of eight names for selection, then they would see the closed list of eight verbs, and so on.
This procedure makes the task demands for the participant more akin to those in an alternate forced choice recognition task.

The closed list sampling and lessened difficulty at retrieval may have encouraged quite different encoding and maintenance strategies when compared to previous studies of memory comparing nouns to other lexical categories.
Thus, it is unclear how generally comparable these findings are with other studies of sentence recall.

In this paper we manipulate noun position in an immediate sentence recall task to determine whether previous within-clause primacy and recency effects were due to clause-based memory organization or to noun position.

Clauses varied internally by syntactic structure, widening the combinatory possibilities for each sentence and allowing placement of more varied lexical categories in clause final and clause initial positions.
We also controlled several other factors which may have influenced positional effects in prior multi-clause recall studies.
Sentence presentation was done with isochronous rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) to prevent use of explicit prosody and other timing cues that might encourage grouping.
The critical sentences used were all 12 orthographic words long and biclausal.

To prevent grouping by a simple counting metric, like number of words, clause lengths varied, with half of the sentences being composed of a five-word clause followed by a seven-word clause, and the other half composed of a seven-word clause followed by a five-word clause.
Finally, the stimuli used here are conceptually coherent within and across clauses.
The data reported here come from 49 self-reported native English speakers.

Forty-one participants were recruited on Prolific and paid for their time, and the remaining eight were recruited from undergraduate linguistics courses at the University of Maryland, College Park and received course credit for their participation.
Demographic information beyond self-reported native language was not collected.
Written consent was acquired from each subject, and the procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Maryland.

Following the maintenance period, participants were prompted to orally recall the list with the word RECORDING.
The recall period was self-paced, and participants clicked a button labeled 'Continue' to move on to the next trial.

After giving their informed consent and testing their microphone's audio collection quality, participants read a short description of the task and then completed four practice trials, consisting of two noun lists and two sentences.
Participants were instructed that they should attempt to recall stimuli word for word as accurately as possible, though imperfections were to be expected.
To encourage the attempted retrieval of as much material as possible, participants were told that they were allowed to say the word "skip" to fill in words that they could not recall.
Once practice trials were completed participants were reminded of their task and told to continue to the main trials.
Stimulus presentation was fully randomized per participant.
Participants were given 10 equally spaced self-paced breaks during the main trials.
The experiment took around 45 minutes on average to complete, ranging from 33 to 75 minutes.
Participants' voice recordings were transcribed using the AssemblyAI API (accessed January through May, 2026), then transcription texts were normalized and scored.

Serial recall accuracy scores reported here use the 'adjacency' scoring method from Baddeley et al. (2009) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jc1GyS where an item is scored as correct if it is produced correctly relative to an item adjacent in the input list.

(2009)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jc1GyS">,</ref> where an item is scored as correct if it is produced correctly relative to an item adjacent in the input list.

text.text: This is essentially a bigram scoring method, where items are scored relative to the bigrams they participate in.
Here, absolute serial order is only taken into account for scoring the beginning and final items in a sequence.
Otherwise, an item is correct if and only if it was produced correctly relative to another correct item.

For instance, with the input sequence ABCDE, a response such as CBADE would only be scored correct for positions D and E, since E was produced finally, and D was produced adjacent to E. The item A in the response is incorrect since it was not produced first, and none of the other items were produced correctly adjacent to another correct item.
Note that simple intrusions at non-initial and non-final positions are not penalized under this scoring system, since intrusions only disrupt a single adjacency relation.
For example, with the input sequence ABCDE, the response ABXCDE removes the adjacency relation between B -C but does not affect adjacency between C -D, meaning this position can be scored as correct.
However, if another element intrudes between C -D, such as in ABXCYDE, then C will be marked incorrect, since it does not retain either of the adjacency relations seen in the input string.

This may be considered a more stringent case of the relative order scoring methodhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8i3Wj8 as recommended for serial recall tasks by Addis & Kahana (2004) , where the relative order relation is limited to direct adjacency.

text.text: The ROPE is an interval in the space of parameter estimates where estimates that land within this interval may be considered to be of negligible magnitude.
We can then compare the ROPE interval to the full interval of our estimated parameter posterior and quantify what percentage of these estimates are found in the ROPE.

While it is statistically more appropriate to interpret posteriors over parameters as continuous measures of evidence for a hypothesis, we consider a simplified binary decision rule: if 2.5% or less of the estimated posterior interval overlaps with the ROPE, then we have strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis.
If 97.5% or more of the posterior falls within the ROPE, then we have strong evidence for the null hypothesis (see Makowski et al. 2019 for more details on ROPE analyses).

In this experiment we examined the relative contributions of both abstract clause boundaries and lexical category to serial recall accuracy.
We reported two main findings.
First, we found no evidence for clause-internal primacy and recency when these positions were not occupied by nouns.

Modeling confirmed that the scalloped shapes seen in the descriptive curves were driven by nominal boundary elements, which we expected to demonstrate an independent recall boost above non-nominal elements.
The noun boost to recall was found to hold across all nouns presented within the stimulus sentences, when compared to other open class lexical categories.
Second, additional modeling revealed that recall of items within initial clauses was more accurate than that of items within final clauses.

Although this effect was in the opposite direction from the benefit for recent clauses that was observed in previous studies (Jarvellahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?1IezOu 1971 (Jarvella, , 1979;; Jarvella & Herman, 1972) , this overall effect of clause membership does suggest that clause boundaries delimit some aspects of retrieval accuracy.

text.text: Taken together, these results suggest that while clauses may serve as chunks in memory, most observed serial position effects within sentences of natural language have been confounded with better recall performance for nouns in general.

text.text: While this connection is intuitive, it is of practical and theoretical importance to clarify where these connections hold, and where they break down.

One influential form of evidence for a relationship between clauses and memory units was observations of primacy and recency within clauses in the recall of multiclausal sentences, mirroring those observed in the recall of chunked word lists.
Here, we have shown that these effects may have been confounded by simpler lexical category differences, the placement of nouns at the beginnings and endings of clauses.

The results of our serial recall experiment showed that when nominal and non-nominal boundary positions were directly compared, apparent clause-internal recency and primacy peaks were driven by nominal element placement only.

Our results do reveal some evidence that clause boundaries delimit aspects of retrieval, however, as we found a significant effect of clause placement on accuracy overall such that first clauses were recalled much more accurately than second clauses.
The recall benefit we observe for nouns replicates some past findings and renews the question of the mechanisms behind superior noun memory.

In this article we aimed to examine a particular interaction between chunking and sentence memory, whereby the first and final words of clauses within a sentence are recalled with greater accuracy than these non-boundary words.

This metric has been used before in the study of sentence recall, where scalloped curves over clauses led to claims that clauses serve as chunks (Aaronson & Scarborough, 1977; Jarvella, 1979; Marslen-Wilson & Tyler, 1976; Roverud et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This metric has been used before in the study of sentence recall, where scalloped curves over clauses led to claims that clauses serve as chunks <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Aaronson & Scarborough, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Jarvella, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Marslen-Wilson & Tyler, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Roverud et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We were unable to show clear evidence for clausal primacy and recency when the boundary positions did not contain nominal elements.
However, we do not take this to indicate that clauses are not chunks in recall.
Rather, we argue that serial position effects are poorly suited measurements for sentential material, given the representational affordances of grammatical dependencies.

There is a mass of previous research implicating clauses as chunks that does not rely on serial accuracy measurements, suggesting again that measurements of chunking that do not rely on primacy and recency are better suited to characterizing sentence chunks.

We also argue that it is plausible that a kind of dependency-based cueing granted by grammatical organization may have led to our null effects of sentence-medial primacy and recency, by flattening out the serial recall curves within clauses.
These issues are covered in turn below.

One alternative measure for evaluating chunking relies on the assumption that chunks are unitized groups of items such that recall accuracy for one item within the chunk predicts better recall for other items in that chunk.
If clauses serve as chunks, then they should demonstrate unitized retrieval, where successful retrieval of any part of the clause indicates successful retrieval of its entirety.
Testing this, Gilchrist et al. (2008) used the metric of chunk completion, examining how often participants could complete the entirety of a chunk, conditional on recall of just a single element.
text.formatted: Testing this, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Gilchrist et al. (2008)</ref> used the metric of chunk completion, examining how often participants could complete the entirety of a chunk, conditional on recall of just a single element.

text.text: They gave older and younger adults multi-clausal spoken sentences for immediate recall and found that older adults on average recalled fewer clauses than younger adults.

However, the completeness of the recalled clauses did not differ between groups, because if participants could retrieve a single word from a clause, it was highly probable that they would retrieve all words of that clause.
This is suggestive of chunking since it points towards the retrieval of unitized encodings limited to clause boundaries.
Similar findings held in development as well, where younger children can be shown to access fewer clauses than older children, but show an equal level of clause completion (Gilchrist et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Similar findings held in development as well, where younger children can be shown to access fewer clauses than older children, but show an equal level of clause completion <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Gilchrist et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: From these data it seems that short-term sentence capacity is defined over clauses, rather than words.

A convergent finding to those above comes from comprehension accuracy of multi-clausal sentences. Roberts & Gibson (2002) tested whether the number of clauses or the number of discourse referents in a sentence affected comprehenders' ability to accurately respond to simple questions.
text.formatted: A convergent finding to those above comes from comprehension accuracy of multi-clausal sentences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Roberts & Gibson (2002)</ref> tested whether the number of clauses or the number of discourse referents in a sentence affected comprehenders' ability to accurately respond to simple questions.

text.text: They compared different clause types containing varying numbers of noun phrases, and found that the number of clauses in a presented sentence strongly affected accuracy of a comprehension question asked immediately after, but that the number of noun phrases did not.
Despite some clause types containing more discourse referents (noun phrases), it seemed again that this internal complexity did not matter, but rather the number of clauses itself did.

More recent work has aimed to situate chunking-by-clause within the temporal context model of Howard & Kahana (2002). Balachandran et al. (2025) find evidence in recall and recognition of multi-clausal sentences that clause boundaries serve to delimit temporal contexts, creating episodes that closely encode within-clause content while distancing whole-clause episodes from one another.

text.text: None of the measurements used in these studies rely on changes of serial accuracy as a function of distance to a chunk boundary for their conclusions, an analytical choice that we believe is well suited to study chunks within sentences.
To understand why non-serial measurements of chunking-by-clause have proven more appropriate, we must consider how linear order in sentences is different from linear order in lists.
Consider as an example the placement of adjectives in English.
The vast majority of adjectives are prenominal, placed linearly before their associated noun, such as "wet capybara" or "cute hamster".
This means that in the recall of a grammatical sentence, retrieval of an adjective will often serve to constrain the serial position following it to be a noun.
The same is true for all lexical categories; retrieval of any word in a sentence will serve as a cue to the items that followed (and preceded) it, facilitating accurate recall.
In fact, even languages with so-called free word orders demonstrate certain sequential constraints, which may be universal across languages (Cinque, 2005; Legate, 2001).
text.formatted: In fact, even languages with so-called free word orders demonstrate certain sequential constraints, which may be universal across languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Cinque, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Legate, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, words within a sentence demonstrate a kind of sequential redundancy that is not shared with word lists.
What mechanism underlies these sequential redundancies?
One possible explanation is that grammaticality augments short term memory by means of consistent intrasentential cueing from one word to another.
Retrieval of an adjective cues the retrieval of the noun it holds a dependency with, and retrieval of a noun cues the need for a verb or preposition to introduce that noun.

Note that this description is abstracted away from specific lexical items, which belong to the class of nouns, verbs, etc., but it is also the case that retrieving specific lexical items will often serve to constrain other surrounding items, at least with naturalistic sentences.
In stimuli without semantic anomalies, successfully retrieving a noun like read will often serve to constrain a following object noun to be something that is readable, a magazine, a book, and so on.
It may even be the case that comprehenders can retrieve single, specific words, which can then be used to infer the abstract structure around them.
These constraints are not limited by position, meaning the effects of redundant cueing apply at every serial position.
Both of these boosts, to order and item memory, are contributions from long term memory, and it is this support that distinguishes grammatical strings from randomly ordered strings.

How much long term memory support comes at encoding (Bonhage et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Wv8axk 2014) rather than retrieval, as in redintegration (Jones & Farrell, 2018) , is a question beyond the current article.
text.formatted: How much long term memory support comes at encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bonhage et al., 2014)</ref> rather than retrieval, as in redintegration <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Jones & Farrell, 2018)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Wv8axk">,</ref> is a question beyond the current article.

text.text: Regardless of the locus of this long term memory support, these serial redundancies have the effect of muting serial position effects in sentence chunks, since successful retrieval of first and final chunk elements is conditional on retrieval of other items within those chunks.
This is unlike cases of retrieval from list chunks, where there are no within-chunk redundancies.
We can conclude from this that detection of serial position effects as a chunking metric is much more appropriate when applied to word lists than when applied to sentences.
In this study we discovered evidence of augmented recall performance of nominal elements over non-nominal elements embedded within sentences.
We show that the superiority of noun recall could explain previous findings of primacy and recency within clauses of multi-clausal sentences.
Given this fact, the placement of nouns serves as a confound in the study of sentence memory position effects.
We briefly consider future avenues for deconfounding noun memory and more general sentence memory.

It is important to note that findings of noun superiority are not novel in recall and recognition, and similar effects have been noted for decades in psycholinguistics and cognitive psychology. Reynolds & Flagg (1976) review much of this early literature, along with the results of five novel studies examining noun and verb memory specifically.
text.formatted: It is important to note that findings of noun superiority are not novel in recall and recognition, and similar effects have been noted for decades in psycholinguistics and cognitive psychology. <ref type="bibr">Reynolds & Flagg (1976)</ref> review much of this early literature, along with the results of five novel studies examining noun and verb memory specifically.

text.text: The authors appeal to a complex interaction between levels-of-processing that differs between nouns and verbs, pointing towards differences at encoding and maintenance.
Recent research into noun and verb recognition from Earles & Kersten (2017) finds that nouns are recognized far more accurately than verbs embedded in short sentences.
text.formatted: Recent research into noun and verb recognition from <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Earles & Kersten (2017)</ref> finds that nouns are recognized far more accurately than verbs embedded in short sentences.

text.text: These authors hypothesize that it is the difference in specificity of meaning between verbs and nouns that leads to their different statuses in memory.
Despite the long-standing open questions of noun memory, there is currently no dominant theoretical explanation for this noun accuracy boost.
First, it is important to distinguish extrinsic and intrinsic features of particular nouns within sentences.
While some research has emphasized a general, intrinsic, noun memory benefit, it is important to note that not all nouns within a sentence bear the same relation to that sentence.

It may be the case that nouns bearing particular relations will demonstrate different levels of memory accuracy, an extrinsic factor having to do with the relation a noun participates in, rather than the noun itself. Chromý and Vojvodić (2024) presented participants with simple, unambiguous declarative sentences containing four nouns, such as "An older retiree read the newspaper on Sunday in the library": one subject noun (retiree), one direct object noun (newspaper), one temporal noun (Sunday), and one locative noun (library).

text.text: Sentences were immediately followed by simple comprehension questions targeting different nouns, e.g.
"What did the retiree read?", "When did the retiree read the newspaper?", or "Where did the retiree read the newspaper?".

Here we focus on the results of unmarked word order sentences: when questions targeted direct objects of verbs, accuracy was significantly higher than when questions targeted adjunct nouns, such as in temporal or locative prepositional phrases.

The authors argue that this arises from variable weighting of information over the course of sentence processing, such that higher degrees of attention are paid to words encoding "core" semantic information, such as arguments.

We note, however, that Chromy and https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?SK12PT (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XdpHTO) task and scoring metric was somewhat different from those used in verbatim serial recall studies and therefore might emphasize gist-level over verbatim retrieval (Aaronson, 1976).

text.text: Regarding intrinsic noun properties, it may be the case that nouns are memorized more accurately because they tend to be concrete, animate, imageable, or some combination of these.
We note that the key nouns used in the experiment presented were quite concrete, matching the concrete nouns of Roverud et al. (2020).
text.formatted: We note that the key nouns used in the experiment presented were quite concrete, matching the concrete nouns of <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Roverud et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: An explanation of noun superiority that appeals to these factors would need to carefully avoid conflating lexical class, a grammatical notion, with facts about concepts.
Taking concreteness as an example, a simple discriminating illustration can be made with the nominalizations of verbs, whereby a verbal stem like destroy can be made into a noun like destruction.
This nominalization is demonstrably a noun, as it can follow an article and by followed by an of phrase, as in "the destruction of the city".
The syntactic distributional facts verify its grammatical noun status, and yet the word destruction does not denote a concrete entity.
Discrimination of these factors in the other direction could come from non-nominal but concrete and imageable words.
Words like blue, loud, fuzzy, and stinky refer to concrete, sensory properties, but are adjectival.
It is then, in principle, possible to separate the factors of concreteness and lexical category in memory.
To our knowledge, experiments in this vein have not been conducted.
As reviewed this far, no theory of noun memory superiority has considered all of the relevant data.

Further research in this area will very likely need to disentangle many of the underlying factors discussed here, such as event reference (as in nominalizations), conceptual factors such as concreteness and animacy, specificity in meaning, and grammatical relations.

While it is likely implausible to assume that these factors can be completely orthogonalized, efforts in large scale word norming studies may be leveraged to approach experimental separation of these variables (Brysbaert et al., 2019; Brysbaert & New, 2009; VanArsdall & Blunt, 2022).
text.formatted: While it is likely implausible to assume that these factors can be completely orthogonalized, efforts in large scale word norming studies may be leveraged to approach experimental separation of these variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Brysbaert et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Brysbaert & New, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">VanArsdall & Blunt, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such a separation could be used to better characterize the superiority of nouns in memory, which would allow chunking researchers to create better tests of the effects of grouping in natural language.
If it is true, as we have claimed, that primacy and recency within clauses cannot be directly measured in general, this raises the question of whether they contribute to clause recall at all.

We propose a nuanced synthesis of our results and the larger memory literature, and suggest that it may still be that primacy and recency are mnemonic factors at play during retrieval of grammatical utterances, but that their effects are obscured by the structure of the data.
While primacy and recency may be laws that apply to any retrieved chunk, even those within sentences, their effects can be muted by other features of the chunk.

As has been discussed here at length, any item in a particular serial position within an utterance of natural language is confounded by the grammatical, lexical, and semantic properties of that utterance, as well as statistical regularities within and across these properties.

If memory researchers could generate stimuli that control for these factors in a way that allows direct measurement of primacy and recency, we predict that serial position effects would be measurable.
This hypothesis is in line with theories suggesting that serial position effects are "laws of memory", consequences of the human memory system in general (Kahana et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This hypothesis is in line with theories suggesting that serial position effects are "laws of memory", consequences of the human memory system in general <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Kahana et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: An alternative explanation for our failure to observe clause-level primacy and recency effects for non-nominal elements is that chunk-level primacy and recency effects are not a domain-general memory phenomena, but are rather specific to relatively unstructured material, such as lists of words or digits.

This may be dispreferred on theoretical grounds, if one pursues a theory in which serial position effects are simply reflexes of the architecture of encoding and retrieval, and cannot be deactivated for some stimuli and not others (Farrell, 2012).
text.formatted: This may be dispreferred on theoretical grounds, if one pursues a theory in which serial position effects are simply reflexes of the architecture of encoding and retrieval, and cannot be deactivated for some stimuli and not others <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Farrell, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: We acknowledge that a theory like this would be capable of explaining the data reported here, and that the data cannot currently adjudicate between these two options.
The focus in this article has been on examining parallels between clauses and chunks, though it is plausible that other linguistic representations could be used as chunks in memory.
It may be the case that comprehenders encode entire sentences as single chunks, forgoing the finer grained internal segments.

The exact nature of this holistic sentence representation is unclear, though one consideration with some precedent is that it may be a semantic trace, spanning the entirety of the sentence and unitizing it into a single proposition (Riven & de Almeida, 2021).
text.formatted: The exact nature of this holistic sentence representation is unclear, though one consideration with some precedent is that it may be a semantic trace, spanning the entirety of the sentence and unitizing it into a single proposition <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Riven & de Almeida, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The influential regeneration hypothesis from Potter & Lombardi (Lombardi & Potter, 1992; Potter & Lombardi, 1990 , 1998) takes the stance that comprehenders have explicit access to only an abstract meaning trace; all lexical, structural, and otherwise formal traces are merely implicit and not consciously accessible during recall, though they still have bearing on recall via priming.

text.text: While we believe this stance too strong, it is readily apparent that comprehenders rely on semantic encodings to complete sentence recall tasks, and we assume that this was the case in our study as well, as we took care to create coherent and naturalistic sentences that would avoid biasing participants away from whole sentence encoding.
Sentence-spanning traces need not be characterized as semantic, and it may be the case that the encoding of representations of other qualities could lead to similar behavior.

For instance, it is likely that comprehenders can and do use features of an utterance's form in segmentation for memory as well, one of the most prominent of these features being prosodic boundaries (Simpson & Martin, 2015).
text.formatted: For instance, it is likely that comprehenders can and do use features of an utterance's form in segmentation for memory as well, one of the most prominent of these features being prosodic boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Simpson & Martin, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Using behavioral intuitions, Anurova et al. (2022) found that phonetic factors such as prosodic strength and pause length, as well as clause boundaries, jointly determined where comprehenders annotated chunks.

text.text: Effects of these chunk boundaries during comprehension were also found in simultaneous magneto/electroencephalography data.
Thus, the authors present behavioral and neural evidence that distinct cues to segmentation independently contribute to chunking behavior in on-line comprehension.

A final aspect of the results found in this study is the lack of a clause recency effect, the term applied to the finding that in some memory tasks with multiclausal stimuli, the most recently encountered clause demonstrates an accuracy benefit over all other clauses (Chang, 1980; Gernsbacher et al., 1989; Jarvella, 1979; Lee & Kim, 2009; Marslen-Wilson & Tyler, 1976).

text.text: There was no evidence for clause recency in these data, and in fact the opposite held: there was strong evidence to suggest that initial clauses were recalled with greater accuracy than final clauses.

One possibility is that the 2000ms maintenance period after encoding and before recall in the current design caused participants to shift from a representation that more strongly encoded the final clause, to one that more strongly encoded the first clause.
In the discourse processing literature, Gernsbacher et al. (1989) reported a pattern of findings consistent with this possibility.
text.formatted: In the discourse processing literature, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Gernsbacher et al. (1989)</ref> reported a pattern of findings consistent with this possibility.

text.text: The authors had participants read biclausal sentences and complete a lexical probe task, and found that the timing of the lexical probe task was crucial for determining whether probe responses would be facilitated for nouns in the initial or final clause.

Probes from final clauses that were shown soon after sentence offset demonstrated reaction time facilitation, though probes from initial clauses showed facilitation only when presented 1400ms or more after sentence offset (though see https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?tPEXZ4. Lee & Kim 2009 for conflicting evidence from Korean).

text.text: The authors argue that this shift in retrieval privilege was tied to a kind of integration that occurred across clauses, where a sentence-spanning holistic representation takes the place of disparate clause-spanning representations.

Crucially, this integration takes time, and when probing early enough one can target the unintegrated representation. Ratcliff & McKoon (1989) find a similar transformation in recognition judgments for simple active and passive sentences, discovering that from around 500-700ms, recognition judgments are made based on surface level similarity, but from 700-2000ms judgments are made based on abstract relational information.

text.text: Extending these findings, it seems possible that the use of a longer maintenance period than previous studies altered the profile of recall in the current experiment.

Within this period after encoding, the representation that participants would retrieve was one of an integrated representation of both clauses, with the first clause taking a privileged role in this integrated representation.

Another possibility is that the first-clause accuracy advantage could reflect a rehearsal effect, where the first clause benefits from more rehearsal or elaboration over the course of parsing, leading to a more robust encoding.
This would be a reasonable strategy, as participants were not asked to complete a simultaneous articulation suppression task.

In this study we investigated how accuracy in immediate sentence recall is affected by an item's lexical category and its position within a sentence, building on previous findings that draw parallels between clauses in sentences and chunks in lists.

We failed to replicate previous findings that accuracy at clause boundaries is higher relative to non-boundary positions when the clause boundary positions did not contain nouns, and our results were consistent with prior work in suggesting that serial recall accuracy for nouns is higher than other lexical categories.
Together, these findings suggest that earlier observations of primacy and recency within clauses were confounded by the placement of nouns.

We suggest that while primacy and recency may be at play during the retrieval of clauses, their influence on accuracy will frequently be difficult to detect due to the grammatical constraints of sentence structure which also contribute to retrieval success.
These results motivate further research aimed at better evaluating the chunking strategies available for complex, structured stimuli such as sentences.
